summary: This informational RFC creates an IANA registry for Content Security Policy directives. It fills the registry with the directives defined in the Content Security Policy Level 2 specification, so that new directives can be tracked in one place.

eli5.summary: A web page can be given rules about where its content may come from. This makes an official list of the words used for those rules.

questions: what is the csp directives registry
how to register a csp directive
subtitle: Creates the IANA registry for Content Security Policy directives and seeds it with the 16 directives from CSP Level 2.

tldr.problem: Content Security Policy is an extensible set of directives, and without a registry extensions could collide or go unlisted.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC creates the top-level IANA registry "Content Security Policy Directives" under the Specification Required policy and fills it with the directives defined in CSP Level 2.
tldr.outcome: New directives must be documented in a public specification and registered, with a designated expert reviewing them.

today: RFC 7762 is an Informational RFC from January 2016. The metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why a Directive Registry
sections.content:
The Content Security Policy (CSP) specification defines a mechanism web developers use to control the resources a page can fetch or execute, plus other security-relevant policy decisions. The policy language is an extensible set of directives, each controlling a specific resource type or policy decision.

This RFC establishes a registry so that extensions to CSP are listed and standardized.
sections.eli5: CSP rules are written with special words. An official word list stops two people from using the same word for different things.

sections.title: Registration Requirements
sections.content:
A directive must be documented in a readily available public specification. That documentation MUST fully explain the syntax, intended usage and semantics, to assure interoperable independent implementations and to prevent accidental namespace collisions. Documents defining new directives MUST register them with IANA.

A registration provides the directive name, an ASCII string matching the CSP rule directive-name = 1*( ALPHA / DIGIT / "-" ), and a reference to the specification.
sections.eli5: To add a word, you must write down exactly what it means where anyone can read it, and give IANA the word and the place.

sections.title: Policy and Initial Contents
sections.content:
The policy is "Specification Required", which uses a designated expert. The IESG SHOULD draw experts from the W3C's security community through the liaison.

The expert SHOULD consider that CSP is restrictive, so deploying it is a strict reduction in risk, and should check that a proposed directive does not violate that property. The expert should also balance granular directives against providing only knobs with known security implications.

The initial registry has 16 entries, all referencing the CSP specification: base-uri, child-src, connect-src, default-src, font-src, form-action, frame-ancestors, frame-src, img-src, media-src, object-src, plugin-types, report-uri, sandbox, script-src and style-src.
sections.eli5: A careful reviewer decides which new words get on the list, and mostly checks that a new word cannot make a web page less safe.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The registry does not in itself have security implications, but the directives certainly do. The documents referenced when registering new directives MUST contain detailed security and privacy considerations sections, and SHOULD contain usage information that tells web developers the expected implementation.
sections.eli5: The list is harmless, but each word on it affects safety, so each word's rulebook must explain the risks.
